Thank you for resubmitting your work entitled "Dopaminergic regulation of vestibulo-cerebellar circuits through unipolar brush cells" for further consideration by eLife. Your revised article has been evaluated by Gary Westbrook (Senior Editor) and a Reviewing Editor. The manuscript has been improved but there are some remaining issues that need to be addressed, as outlined below. The most significant concern relates to the magnitude and significance of the dopaminergic effects.

Recommendations for the authors:

While the authors have used state-of-the-art tools and extremely thorough analyses to characterize functional Drd1 expression in UBCs, the ultimate impact on cerebellar function remains unclear. There is consensus that the results are still interesting, both in terms of the new characterizations of UBCs and from the perspective of co-transmission in general. However, the limitations to the conclusions that can be made regarding the impact on cerebellar function need to be stated and discussed more explicitly. In particular, the conditions under which DA release might occur and the extent to which it could affect cerebellar function in vivo need to be clearly discussed. A discussion of the limitations of the slice preparation could also be helpful (For example, these sparse LC inputs might be weak in slice preparation, but could be stronger under particular behavioral circumstances). Please revise the manuscript to make these limitations more explicit as well as responding to the specific comments of the reviewers, below.

Reviewer #1:

The authors addressed my concerns raised in the first submission.

Reviewer #2:

In this revision, Canton-Josh and colleagues have addressed prior reviews thoroughly. The revised manuscript presents an exhaustive set of experiments evaluating dopamine's effects on a subset of UBCs and Purkinje cell feedback to that population.

I support publication of this manuscript. However, I have one minor concern which is the strength of the authors' conclusion that LC is the source of dopamine to UBCs in Lobule X. FIg. 4 shows that hardly any LC neurons were retrogradely labeled by the viral strategy; Fig. 5F shows that lobule X seems uniquely low in LC inputs, compared to the rest of the cerebellum; and Fig. 5G shows a fairly weak GRAB-da response even to 200 pulses of LC neurons. The authors have done an admirable job delineating the possible sources of dopamine here and trying to rule out other options based on their numerous labeling and in situ experiments, and I don't have any other ideas for where this dopamine input might come from. Perhaps the authors could simply acknowledge the relative sparseness here as a consideration in interpretation.

Reviewer #3:

This paper proposes an interesting link between Purkinje cells and UBCs that may be selectively modulated by dopamine coming from locus coeruleus projections. While a tremendous number of state-of-the-art experiments are shown, I remain concerned about the magnitude of the actions of synaptically released DA onto UBCs and the impact downstream to Purkinje cells.

For example, Figure 2 describes the key point that DA accelerates firing in UBCs. The legend of the figure says that the agonist SKF81297 was applied with a 300 ms puff. The effect was a 110% increase over baseline, though with enormous scatter and a total increase of only 2.4 Hz. However, if one looks in the Methods, one finds the following description of how this experiment was performed: "The baseline period lasted ~7 min (20 trials) before we applied SKF81297. To activate Drd1 receptors we puff applied SKF81297 (500 µM) using a 300 ms long PicoSpritzer puff (Parker Hannifin, Hollis, NH). The drug was applied once per trial (20 s ITI) for a 10-minute period (30 trials). We continued recording after drug application for a 10-minute (30 trials) washout period." Thus, we are not dealing with an acute effect of dopamine, as implied perhaps by saying it was a 300 ms puff, but rather a gradual change over 10 minutes of repeated applications. It is not uncommon that in recording spontaneous activity from small, high resistance cells, spike rates could change over 10 minutes. Moreover, the rate change upon washout of SKF is not shown.

Then the authors repeat this in the presence of SKF plus 3 DrD1 antagonists all mixed together. Why 3 of the same kind of drug? Line 153 says that this manipulation blocked the effect of SKF on Vm and Rin, but the figures 2F,G shows that the differences were not significant ('ns').

The authors responded to my concern about the small size, and therefore low impact, of NMDAR responses by citing vanDorp and de Zeeuw 2014 as support for NMDAR function in UBCs. That must be an error, as that paper showed simply that a mixture of AMPA and NMDA blockers added together eliminated synaptic responses: "In response to five pulses at 200 Hz, a slow EPSC was observed that rose to a maximal amplitude of ~20 pA in ~200 ms in these two cells. Bath coapplication of NMDAR antagonist D-APV and AMPAR antagonist CNQX abolished the fast response and the subsequent slow wave, confirming their synaptic nature (gray traces)." Thus nothing can be concluded from that experiment about the receptor subtypes mediating the different parts of the EPSC.

Moreover, the NMDAR experiments remain concerning. In Figure 2L-O why is the NMDAR current smaller in response to uncaging than synaptic stimulation? It should be the other way around, since the exogenous glutamate reaches a larger area than a synapse. Also, are the same data represented in N and O? There appear to be several responses over 15 pA in SKF for O but not for panel N.

Figure 4 retrograde rabies experiment labeled just a few LC neurons, and in the figure (4C, far right) these are very hard to see convincingly. So, I feel that this is weak evidence for this projection being important physiologically.

Figure 5 GRABda showed a large response to electrical stimulation of fibers. Yet ChR2 activation of LC fibers caused a weak response, in 5/20 cells, and in less than half of the trials. The best evidence so far that LC projects to Lobe X is from the experiment in which the AAV1-FlexFRT-ChR2 virus was injected into the LC of TH-FLPO mouse and then image lobe X. Yet in Figure 5F it seems that there is no label in lobe X. Fig5S1 has a higher power image of lobe X that should be moved to the main figure, yet it shows that the labeled fibers are in the molecular layer, not where the UBCs are. Additionally, we still do not know if such stimulation of LC cells would lead to an ionic current or NMDAR modulation in UBCs. ChR2 stim of ChR2 expressing LC axons barely increased firing (increase of 1.2 Hz).

Figure 6 – Activation of all of the DrD1 UBCs at the same time with ChR2 can sometimes increase or decrease the firing rate of Purkinje cells, but usually does nothing.

Figure 7 – Activating Purkinje cells causes unreliable IPSCs in UBCs with long latency. In 11/24 cells they saw IPSCs. In 60% of trials of 100 light pulses there was at least one IPSC.

claims.source: This increase could be blocked by bath application of Drd2 antagonist, as expected for this sensor (Figure 5D) (1 µM L-741,626, n = 10 cells, 4.88-fold reduction in peak amplitude, paired t-test, p=0.002).
claims.evidence: Measured from two-photon imaging showing 4.88-fold reduction in GRABDA2h response with L-741,626 (Figure 5D).

claims.claim: LC axons spread broadly across all layers of the cerebellum.
claims.source: Anterograde labeling of axons from the LC to the cerebellum. Left: Injection of AAV1-FLEX-FRT-ChR2-mCherry into the LC shows axons spreading broadly across all layers of the cerebellum (n = 2 mice).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by anterograde viral tracing showing mCherry+ axons throughout cerebellar layers (Figure 5F).

claims.claim: Optogenetic activation of LC axons (200 pulses, 39 Hz) elicits time-locked increases in GRABDA2h fluorescence in a subset of UBCs (5/20 cells).
claims.source: We imaged GRABDA2h fluorescence in UBCs in the acute slice while optogenetically activating LC axons (200 pulses, 39 Hz, 2 ms pulses, 460 nm). In each experiment, the absence of TH+ Pkj cell labeling was confirmed to ensure selective LC targeting without overflow of ChR2 expression into the cerebellum. We found time-locked increases of GRABDA2h fluorescence in UBCs in response to optical stimulation in a subset of UBCs (n = 2 mice, 5/20 cells) (Figure 5G–H).
claims.evidence: Measured from two-photon imaging of GRABDA2h during optogenetic LC stimulation (Figure 5G-H).

claims.claim: Optically evoked GRABDA2h transients in UBCs have an average success rate of ~40% across responding cells.
claims.source: Optically evoked GRABDA2h transients had an average success rate of ~40% across responding cells.
claims.evidence: Calculated from imaging data of optogenetic LC stimulation experiments (Figure 5G-H).

claims.claim: Bath application of Drd1 agonist SKF81297 (10 µM) increases firing rate in cell-attached recordings of Drd1+ UBCs.
claims.source: First, we performed cell-attached recordings of Drd1+ UBCs, collected data during a baseline period, and then applied 10 µm SKF81297 (Figure 5I). Consistent with our whole-cell current clamp recordings, we measured an increase in spontaneous firing rate in tdT+ UBCs in response to Drd1 agonist (Figure 5J) (n = 10 cells, paired Wilcoxon signed rank test, p=0.002).
claims.evidence: Measured from cell-attached recordings comparing baseline and SKF81297 periods (Figure 5I-J).

claims.claim: Optogenetic stimulation of LC fibers (20 Hz) increases firing rate of Drd1+ UBCs by 1.2 Hz (26% above baseline) in cell-attached recordings.
claims.source: We measured a small but significant increase in the firing rate of Drd1+ UBCs in response to LC fiber stimulation (Figure 5L–M) (1.2 Hz increase, 26% above baseline, n = 8 cells, paired Wilcoxon signed rank test, p=0.02).
claims.evidence: Measured from cell-attached recordings during optogenetic LC stimulation with adrenergic and glutamatergic receptors blocked (Figure 5L-M).

claims.claim: Optogenetic stimulation of LC fibers does not significantly change UBC firing rate in the presence of Drd1 antagonist.
claims.source: In a separate set of experiments with Drd1 antagonist (5 µM SCH39166) present in the bath, we measured no statistically significant changes in firing rate.
claims.evidence: Measured from cell-attached recordings during optogenetic LC stimulation with Drd1 antagonist present (Figure 5L-M).

claims.claim: Optogenetic activation of Drd1+ UBCs causes ChR2+ UBCs to respond with 2-5 action potentials per pulse.
claims.source: We stimulated UBCs with a train of LED pulses (460 nm, 10 Hz, 50 pulses, 1 ms pulse width). Each pulse caused a small burst of action potentials (2–5 APs).
claims.evidence: Measured from cell-attached recordings of ChR2+ UBCs during optogenetic stimulation (Figure 6B-C).

claims.claim: UBCs are more likely to respond with multiple spikes to a pulse at the beginning of a train than at the end.
claims.source: UBCs were more likely to respond with multiple spikes to a pulse at the beginning of the train than at the end (Figure 6B–C).
claims.evidence: Measured from cell-attached recordings showing decreased spike number across pulse train (Figure 6C).

claims.claim: Optogenetic activation of Drd1+ UBCs does not significantly alter average Purkinje cell firing rate.
claims.source: Pkj cells did not significantly alter their average firing rate on trials with optogenetic stimulation (Figure 6D).
claims.evidence: Measured from cell-attached recordings of Pkj cells during UBC optogenetic stimulation (Figure 6D).

claims.claim: In a subset of Purkinje cells, optogenetic stimulation of UBCs causes a brief pause in firing during the 500 ms period after stimulus onset.
claims.source: However, in a subset of Pkj cells, stimulation caused a brief pause in firing during the 500 ms period after the beginning of the optogenetic stimulus (Figure 6E).
claims.evidence: Measured from cell-attached recordings showing decreased firing rate in subset of Pkj cells (Figure 6E-G).

claims.claim: Approximately 28% of Purkinje cells (8/28) are 'Pausers' in response to UBC optogenetic activation.
claims.source: The majority of Pkj cells (18/28) did not significantly alter their firing rate, ~ 28% of cells were 'Pausers' (8/28) and 7% of Pkj cells qualified as 'Bursters' (2/28) (Figure 6F–G).
claims.evidence: Quantified from cell-attached recordings of Pkj cells during UBC optogenetic stimulation (Figure 6F-G).

claims.claim: Approximately 7% of Purkinje cells (2/28) are 'Bursters' in response to UBC optogenetic activation.
claims.source: The majority of Pkj cells (18/28) did not significantly alter their firing rate, ~ 28% of cells were 'Pausers' (8/28) and 7% of Pkj cells qualified as 'Bursters' (2/28) (Figure 6F–G).
claims.evidence: Quantified from cell-attached recordings of Pkj cells during UBC optogenetic stimulation (Figure 6F-G).

claims.claim: Purkinje cells with lower EPSC/IPSC ratios are more likely to pause after UBC activation.
claims.source: We calculated the EPSC/IPSCs charge ratio and plotted it against change in firing rate z-score (Figure 6I). Neurons with lower EPSC/IPSC ratios were more likely to pause after the onset of stimulation, suggesting that in these cells the relatively larger inhibitory current favored the pause.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by correlation analysis showing R2=0.63 between EPSC/IPSC ratio and firing rate z-score (Figure 6I).

claims.claim: 11 out of 24 UBCs (46%) receive short latency synaptic input from Purkinje cells.
claims.source: In UBC voltage clamp experiments, we found that 11/24 UBCs received short latency synaptic input from Pkj cells (Figure 7D).
claims.evidence: Quantified from voltage clamp recordings of UBCs during optogenetic Pkj cell stimulation (Figure 7D).

claims.claim: UBCs receiving IPSCs from Purkinje cells have a per trial success ratio of 0.64 on average.
claims.source: Cells with successful evoked IPSCs had a per trial success ratio of 0.64 on average (Figure 7D).
claims.evidence: Calculated from voltage clamp recordings showing successful IPSC responses (Figure 7D).

claims.claim: Optically evoked IPSCs in UBCs from Purkinje cells have an average amplitude of 91 pA ± 24.
claims.source: There was significant variability in the amplitude (91 pA, ± 24) (Figure 7H) and timing (9.4 ms ±2.4) (Figure 7E) of optically evoked IPSCs, with some cells exhibiting large currents over the entire stimulation period and others responding with a single large IPSC at the onset of stimulation.
claims.evidence: Measured from voltage clamp recordings of UBCs during optogenetic Pkj cell stimulation (Figure 7H).

claims.claim: Optically evoked IPSCs in UBCs from Purkinje cells have an average latency of 9.4 ms ± 2.4.
claims.source: There was significant variability in the amplitude (91 pA, ± 24) (Figure 7H) and timing (9.4 ms ±2.4) (Figure 7E) of optically evoked IPSCs, with some cells exhibiting large currents over the entire stimulation period and others responding with a single large IPSC at the onset of stimulation.
claims.evidence: Measured from voltage clamp recordings showing time to first IPSC (Figure 7E).

claims.claim: Application of gabazine (10 µM) abolishes evoked IPSCs in UBCs from Purkinje cell stimulation.
claims.source: In a subset of UBCs (n = 9 cells) (Figure 7F–G), we flowed in 10 µM gabazine to ensure the measured currents were due to GABAA channel opening. Application of gabazine abolished all evoked currents (Figure 7H).
claims.evidence: Measured from voltage clamp recordings showing elimination of IPSCs with gabazine (Figure 7F-H).

claims.claim: Cerebellar activity plays a critical function in fine motor learning.
claims.source: Cerebellar activity plays a critical function in fine motor learning (Kalmbach et al., 2010; Raymond and Lisberger, 1998; Woodruff-pak, 1993).
claims.evidence: Cited from prior literature (Kalmbach et al., 2010; Raymond and Lisberger, 1998; Woodruff-pak, 1993).

claims.claim: Important anatomical, molecular, and functional differences between cerebellar lobules are beginning to emerge.
claims.source: The cerebellum is defined by its clearly organized cytoarchitecture; however, important anatomical, molecular, and functional differences between lobules are beginning to emerge.
claims.evidence: General statement about emerging research trends in cerebellar neuroscience.

claims.claim: Unipolar brush cells (UBCs) are glutamatergic interneurons enriched in the granular layer of vestibulo-cerebellum.
claims.source: One key difference between cerebellar lobules is the distribution of unipolar brush cells (UBCs), glutamatergic interneurons enriched in the granular layer of vestibulo-cerebellum, which is known to be involved in processing vestibular sensory input (Mugnaini and Floris, 1994).
claims.evidence: Cited from prior literature (Mugnaini and Floris, 1994).

claims.claim: Vestibulo-cerebellum is involved in processing vestibular sensory input.

claims.evidence: Cited from prior literature (Mugnaini and Floris, 1994).

claims.claim: UBCs reside in the granular layer and receive inputs from mossy fibers.
claims.source: UBCs reside in the granular layer and receive inputs from mossy fibers.

claims.evidence: Established anatomical knowledge about UBC connectivity.

claims.claim: UBCs are recurrently connected.
claims.source: Since UBCs are recurrently connected, they are poised to amplify and temporally extend the influence of excitatory inputs into the cerebellum (Requarth and Sawtell, 2014).
claims.evidence: Cited from prior literature (Requarth and Sawtell, 2014).

claims.claim: UBCs are poised to amplify and temporally extend the influence of excitatory inputs into the cerebellum.
claims.source: Since UBCs are recurrently connected, they are poised to amplify and temporally extend the influence of excitatory inputs into the cerebellum (Requarth and Sawtell, 2014).
claims.evidence: Cited from prior literature (Requarth and Sawtell, 2014).

claims.claim: UBCs receiving a single mossy fiber input could form a 'labeled line' input to the granular layer, helping distinguish between inputs from semicircular canals and vestibular nuclei.

claims.evidence: Cited from prior literature (Balmer and Trussell, 2019).

claims.claim: UBCs were discovered in the late 1970s.
claims.source: The relatively recent discovery of UBCs in the late 1970s (Altman and Bayer, 1977) and characterization in the 1990s (Mugnaini and Floris, 1994), their sparseness in the cerebellum, and the lack of tools to isolate them have limited our understanding of their functional connectivity.
claims.evidence: Cited from prior literature (Altman and Bayer, 1977).

claims.claim: UBCs were characterized in the 1990s.

claims.evidence: Cited from prior literature (Mugnaini and Floris, 1994).

claims.claim: Norepinephrine regulates cerebellar output.
claims.source: While it is clear that norepinephrine (NE) regulates cerebellar output, the mechanistic details of neuromodulatory effects for other amines remain poorly understood (Basile and Dunwiddie, 1984; Carey and Regehr, 2009; Lanore et al., 2019; Lippiello et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: Cited from prior literature (Basile and Dunwiddie, 1984; Carey and Regehr, 2009; Lanore et al., 2019; Lippiello et al., 2015).

claims.claim: Dopamine type 1 receptor (Drd1) is expressed within the granular layer of the cerebellum.
claims.source: Previous reports posit the expression of dopamine type 1 receptor (Drd1) within the granular layer of the cerebellum (Locke et al., 2018; Panagopoulos et al., 1993).
claims.evidence: Cited from prior literature (Locke et al., 2018; Panagopoulos et al., 1993).

claims.claim: Several groups have previously reported dopaminergic projections from the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc) and the ventral tegmental area (VTA) targeting the cerebellar cortex of rats and monkeys.
claims.source: Additionally, several groups have previously reported dopaminergic projections from the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc) and the ventral tegmental area (VTA), targeting the cerebellar cortex of rats and monkeys (Melchitzky and Lewis, 2000; Panagopoulos et al., 1991).
claims.evidence: Cited from prior literature (Melchitzky and Lewis, 2000; Panagopoulos et al., 1991).

claims.claim: Recent work in mice did not find evidence for projections from midbrain dopaminergic nuclei to the cerebellum.
claims.source: Yet, recent work in mice did not find evidence for projections from midbrain dopaminergic nuclei to the cerebellum.
claims.evidence: Reference to recent unpublished or published work, context suggests citation but none provided in this sentence.

claims.claim: Vestibulo-cerebellar Purkinje cells express tyrosine hydroxylase (TH), the rate-limiting enzyme in the classical dopamine synthesis pathway.
claims.source: Vestibulo-cerebellar Pkj cells express TH, the rate-limiting enzyme in the classical dopamine (DA) synthesis pathway (Abbott et al., 1996; Huang et al., 2016; Sawada et al., 2004; Takada et al., 1993).
claims.evidence: Cited from prior literature (Abbott et al., 1996; Huang et al., 2016; Sawada et al., 2004; Takada et al., 1993).

claims.claim: Purkinje cells release dopamine onto their own dendrites, which express dopamine type 2 receptor (Drd2).
claims.source: One prior report details a dendritic release of dopamine by Pkj cells onto their own dendrites, expressing dopamine type 2 receptor (Drd2) (Kim et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: Cited from prior literature (Kim et al., 2009).

claims.claim: Locus coeruleus releases dopamine as well as norepinephrine in the hippocampus.
claims.source: A third potential source of cerebellar dopamine is the locus coeruleus (LC), recently demonstrated to release dopamine as well as NE in the hippocampus (Kawahara et al., 2001; Kempadoo et al., 2016; Takeuchi et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: Cited from prior literature (Kawahara et al., 2001; Kempadoo et al., 2016; Takeuchi et al., 2016).

claims.claim: The proposed mechanism for dual amine co-release from locus coeruleus is incomplete conversion of dopamine to norepinephrine in the vesicles.
claims.source: The proposed mechanism of action for this dual amine co-release is incomplete conversion of dopamine to NE in the vesicles.
claims.evidence: Inferred from prior literature on LC dopamine/norepinephrine co-release mechanisms.

claims.claim: tdT+ cells in the cerebellar cortex of Drd1-Cre;tdTomato mice are distributed across the cerebellar granular layer and enriched in lobules IX and X of the cerebellar vermis, lobules VIb and VII, and the paraflocculus.
claims.source: Analysis of Drd1-Cre;tdTomato (tdT) expression in the cerebellar cortex revealed numerous small tdT+ cells distributed across the cerebellar granular layer (Figure 1A), enriched in lobules IX and X of the cerebellar vermis, lobules VIb and VII, and the paraflocculus.
claims.evidence: Observed from whole brain imaging of Drd1-Cre;tdT mice (Figure 1A).

claims.claim: Cerebellar tdT+ cells in Drd1-Cre;tdTomato mice possess the morphological features of UBCs: a single large dendritic brush and a medium-sized soma relative to granule cells.
claims.source: Confocal imaging confirmed that cerebellar tdT+ cells possess the morphological features of UBCs: a single large dendritic brush and a medium-sized soma relative to granule cells (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: Observed from confocal imaging of tdT+ cells (Figure 1B).

claims.claim: 65% of mGluR1+ UBCs express tdTomato in Drd1-Cre;tdTomato mice.
claims.source: The mGluR1+ and tdT+ populations did not overlap completely, as only 65% of mGluR1+ UBCs expressed tdT.
claims.evidence: Quantified from immunohistochemistry showing 401/779 mGluR1+ cells express tdT (Figure 1D).

claims.claim: 12.5% of calretinin+ (CR) UBCs express tdTomato in Drd1-Cre;tdTomato mice.
claims.source: Very few tdT+ UBCs belonged to calretinin+ (CR) type: 5.3% of tdT+ UBCs expressed CR, and 12.5% of CR+ UBCs expressed tdT (Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: Quantified from immunohistochemistry showing 48/1235 CR+ cells express tdT (Figure 1E).

claims.claim: In the Drd1-Cre;tdT cross, all cerebellar tdT+ cells are UBCs.
claims.source: Given these data, we infer that in the Drd1-Cre;tdT cross, all cerebellar tdT+ cells are UBCs, and that these tdT+ UBCs are a subset of the total UBC population, mostly comprised of mGluR1+ ON UBCs.
claims.evidence: Inferred from data showing all tdT+ cells express Tbr2 (Figure 1C) and have UBC morphology (Figure 1B).

claims.claim: tdT+ UBCs in Drd1-Cre;tdT mice are a subset of the total UBC population, mostly comprised of mGluR1+ ON UBCs.
claims.source: Given these data, we infer that in the Drd1-Cre;tdT cross, all cerebellar tdT+ cells are UBCs, and that these tdT+ UBCs are a subset of the total UBC population, mostly comprised of mGluR1+ ON UBCs.
claims.evidence: Inferred from data showing 35% of Tbr2+ UBCs express tdT (Figure 1C) and 71% of tdT+ cells express mGluR1 (Figure 1D).

claims.claim: A prior report using a different Drd1-Cre mouse line reported the expression of Drd1 receptors in deep cerebellar nuclei.
claims.source: A prior report using a different Drd1-Cre mouse line reported the expression of Drd1 receptors in deep cerebellar nuclei (Locke et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Cited from prior literature (Locke et al., 2018).

claims.claim: In the Drd1-Cre;tdTomato cross used in this study, there is no expression of tdT in the cerebellar nuclei.
claims.source: In contrast, we do not see expression of tdT in the cerebellar nuclei in this transgenic cross.
claims.evidence: Observed from imaging of Drd1-Cre;tdT mice showing no tdT expression in cerebellar nuclei.

claims.claim: Cre recombinase lines can show developmentally regulated expression patterns.
claims.source: Because Cre recombinase lines can show developmentally regulated expression patterns, next we evaluated whether tdT+ UBCs contain Drd1 receptors using fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH) to label tdT and Drd1a mRNA transcripts.
claims.evidence: General knowledge about Cre recombinase line properties.

claims.claim: Most Drd1 UBCs express a low amount of Drd1 transcripts.
claims.source: Most Drd1 UBCs express a low amount of Drd1 transcripts.
claims.evidence: Observed from FISH data showing low abundance of Drd1a transcripts in tdT+ UBCs (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).

claims.claim: Most tdT+ UBCs (70%) increased their firing rate in response to Drd1 activation.
claims.source: Most tdT+ UBCs (70%) increased their firing rate in response to Drd1 activation, as has been reported for Drd1-mediated effects on striatal spiny projection neurons (Lahiri and Bevan, 2020).
claims.evidence: Calculated from current clamp recordings showing 9/13 cells increased firing rate with SKF81297 (Figure 2C-D).

claims.claim: Drd1-mediated effects increase firing rate in striatal spiny projection neurons.
claims.source: Most tdT+ UBCs (70%) increased their firing rate in response to Drd1 activation, as has been reported for Drd1-mediated effects on striatal spiny projection neurons (Lahiri and Bevan, 2020).
claims.evidence: Cited from prior literature (Lahiri and Bevan, 2020).

claims.claim: Quiescent UBCs characterized by hyperpolarized resting membrane potential did not initiate activity in response to Drd1 agonist.
claims.source: Quiescent neurons characterized by hyperpolarized resting membrane potential did not initiate activity in response to pharmacological stimulus.
claims.evidence: Observed from current clamp recordings showing some cells did not respond to SKF81297 (Figure 2C-D).

claims.claim: Drd1 activation increases NMDAR currents in prefrontal cortex neurons.
claims.source: Prior research shows an increase in N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor (NMDAR) currents during the activation of Drd1 receptors on neurons in the prefrontal cortex (Chen et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: Cited from prior literature (Chen et al., 2004).

claims.claim: The measured NMDAR currents in UBCs were blocked by the application of NMDAR antagonist CPP (10 µM).
claims.source: In a subset of experiments, we verified that the measured currents were blocked by the application of NMDAR antagonist CPP (10 µM, n = 5 cells) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by voltage clamp recordings showing elimination of currents with CPP (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G).

claims.claim: UBCs are recurrently connected, so the increase in NMDAR currents may be downstream of a post-synaptic mechanism or a consequence of increased excitability in presynaptic UBCs.
claims.source: Since UBCs are recurrently connected, the increase in NMDAR currents may be downstream of a post-synaptic mechanism or a consequence of increased excitability in presynaptic UBCs.
claims.evidence: Logical inference based on known UBC connectivity and experimental observations.

claims.claim: The increase in NMDAR currents with Drd1 activation in UBCs is consistent with a post-synaptic mechanism of action.
claims.source: NMDAR-mediated currents in response to 1-ms long pulses of 725 nm laser light were compared for experiments with and without 10 µM SKF81297 present in the bath. Current amplitudes increased with Drd1 activation, consistent with a post-synaptic mechanism of action (Figure 2N–O) (51% increase of average amplitude, n = 13 cells, unpaired t-test, p=0.0068).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by glutamate uncaging experiments that bypass presynaptic terminals (Figure 2N-O).

claims.claim: Additional mechanisms beyond NMDAR modulation likely account for observed changes in UBC excitability with Drd1 activation.
claims.source: These experiments support an NMDAR-mediated component to Drd1 activation in UBCs, although given prior findings in the striatum and prefrontal cortex, it is likely that additional mechanisms account for observed changes in excitability (Gorelova and Yang, 2000; Surmeier and Kitai, 1993).
claims.evidence: Inferred from comparison with prior literature (Gorelova and Yang, 2000; Surmeier and Kitai, 1993) and experimental observations.

claims.claim: Dat-Cre;tdT axonal fibers in the cerebellum are morphologically consistent with mossy fiber terminals and are restricted to the granule layer.

LRN neurons are glutamatergic, forming mossy fiber rosettes within the cerebellum (Rajakumar et al., 1992; Wu et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: Observed from imaging showing tdT+ fibers with mossy fiber morphology (Figure 3B inset) and confirmed by retrograde tracing to LRN.

claims.claim: There are no prior reports of LRN neurons expressing proteins required for dopamine synthesis or packaging.
claims.source: There are no prior reports of LRN neurons expressing proteins required for dopamine synthesis or packaging.
claims.evidence: Statement about absence of prior literature on this topic.

claims.claim: TH is expressed in Purkinje cells of vermal lobules IX and X.
claims.source: Next, using FISH and antibody labeling, we confirmed previous reports of TH expression in Pkj cells of vermal lobules IX and X (Figure 3D-F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A; Austin et al., 1992; Sakai et al., 1995; Takada et al., 1993).
claims.evidence: Confirmed by FISH and immunohistochemistry (Figure 3D-F) and cited from prior literature (Austin et al., 1992; Sakai et al., 1995; Takada et al., 1993).

claims.claim: Dopamine release from TH+ Purkinje cells is unlikely.

claims.evidence: Inferred from FISH data showing TH+ Pkj cells lack Ddc, Slc18a2, and Slc6a3 transcripts (Figure 3D-F).

claims.claim: The most likely source of dopamine to the Drd1+ UBCs is the locus coeruleus.
claims.source: Given these anatomical data, the most likely source of dopamine to the Drd1+ UBCs is the LC.
claims.evidence: Inferred from exclusion of SNc/VTA and TH+ Pkj cells, combined with positive evidence for LC projections (Figure 3).

claims.claim: Trans-synaptic tracing with modified rabies virus CVS-N2cΔG allows labeling of all pre-synaptic partners of neurons expressing Cre recombinase.

claims.evidence: Cited from prior literature (Balmer and Trussell, 2019).

claims.evidence: Cited from prior literature (Rogers and Beier, 2021) discussing limitations of rabies virus tracing.

claims.evidence: Cited from prior literature (Houck and Person, 2015; Judd et al., 2021).

claims.evidence: Cited from prior literature (Schwarz et al., 2015; Wall et al., 2013).

claims.claim: GRABDA2h is preferentially activated by dopamine but maintains a slight sensitivity to norepinephrine (dopamine EC50 = 0.13 µM, NE EC50 = 1.7 µM).
claims.source: GRABDA2h is preferentially activated by dopamine, but it maintains a slight sensitivity to NE (dopamine EC50 = 0.13 µM, NE EC50 = 1.7 µM) (Sun et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: Cited from prior literature (Sun et al., 2020) describing GRABDA2h sensor properties.

claims.claim: Drd1 receptors activate Gαs-coupled protein cascades.

claims.evidence: Cited from prior literature (Stoof and Kebabian, 1984; Surmeier and Kitai, 1993).

claims.source: Since Drd1 receptors activate Gαs-coupled protein cascades (Stoof and Kebabian, 1984; Surmeier and Kitai, 1993), and whole-cell recordings can dialyze cytosolic proteins involved in G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) signaling (Lahiri and Bevan, 2020), we decided to use cell-attached recordings to measure potential effect of dopamine release from LC axons.

results.result: Drd1 receptors are expressed in a subset of unipolar brush cells (UBCs) in the mouse cerebellar vermis, specifically in approximately 35% of Tbr2+ UBCs, with 76% of tdT+ UBCs expressing Drd1a mRNA transcripts. These Drd1+ UBCs are predominantly mGluR1+ ON-type UBCs (71%), with minimal overlap with calretinin+ UBCs (5.3%).
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C11-C16, C80-C81, C84-C85, and C89 provide converging evidence from multiple complementary techniques (immunohistochemistry, FISH, confocal imaging) demonstrating Drd1 expression in a specific UBC subpopulation. The quantitative data are internally consistent and supported by appropriate controls and markers (Tbr2, mGluR1, calretinin). The 40-fold enrichment of Drd1a puncta within tdT+ soma (C16) provides strong spatial validation.

results.result: Drd1 activation by SKF81297 increases firing rate in UBCs by 2.48 Hz (110% increase), along with increases in membrane potential and input resistance. This effect is specific to Drd1 receptors, as demonstrated by appropriate antagonist and vehicle controls, though approximately 30% of UBCs (quiescent cells) did not respond.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C17-C21, C90, and C92 demonstrate Drd1-mediated excitability changes with appropriate pharmacological controls (antagonist cocktail and ACSF vehicle). The statistical significance (p=0.02) and effect size (110% increase) are substantial. Controls showing no effect with antagonists (p=0.49) or ACSF (p=0.33) strengthen the specificity claim. The observation of non-responding quiescent cells (C92) adds biological nuance.

results.result: Drd1 activation increases NMDAR-mediated currents in UBCs through a post-synaptic mechanism, with a 15% increase observed with electrical stimulation and a 51% increase with glutamate uncaging. The currents are confirmed as NMDAR-mediated by CPP blockade.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C22-C24, C94, and C96 provide strong evidence for post-synaptic NMDAR modulation using complementary approaches (electrical stimulation and glutamate uncaging). The glutamate uncaging experiment (C23, C24) is particularly convincing as it bypasses presynaptic mechanisms. The CPP control (C94) confirms NMDAR identity. The difference in effect size between electrical stimulation (15%) and uncaging (51%) may reflect network effects or methodological differences but both show the same direction of effect.

results.result: Midbrain dopaminergic nuclei (SNc/VTA) do not project to the cerebellar regions containing Drd1+ UBCs, as demonstrated by absence of retrograde labeling in multiple tracing experiments using both Dat-Cre;tdT mice and Th-Flpo mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C25-C26, C33, C39, and C75 provide consistent negative evidence from multiple independent tracing approaches (CTB-488 retrograde tracing, retrograde AAV, and rabies virus tracing). The observation that Dat-Cre;tdT+ axons in cerebellum originate from LRN (C26) rather than SNc/VTA strengthens the conclusion. This contradicts some prior literature (C74) but is consistent with recent mouse studies (C75).

results.result: TH+ Purkinje cells in lobule X lack the molecular machinery necessary for dopamine synthesis and release, specifically lacking transcripts for Ddc (8/163 cells), Slc18a2 (4/37 cells), and Slc6a3 (4/37 cells), in stark contrast to SNc dopamine neurons where these transcripts are abundant.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C29-C31, C100-C101, and C140 provide compelling FISH data with appropriate positive controls (SNc neurons). The quantitative comparison showing minimal expression in TH+ Pkj cells versus high expression in SNc neurons (e.g., 119/134 SNc neurons express Ddc vs 8/163 Pkj cells) is convincing. This resolves a longstanding question in the field about whether TH+ Purkinje cells can release dopamine.

results.result: The locus coeruleus (LC) is identified as the most likely source of dopamine to Drd1+ UBCs, supported by retrograde tracing showing LC neurons project to lobules IX/X, rabies virus tracing showing sparse LC inputs to Drd1+ UBCs, and exclusion of other potential sources.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C32, C38, C102, and C141 converge on LC as the dopamine source through multiple lines of evidence: retrograde AAV tracing (C32), rabies virus tracing (C38), and process of elimination (C102). However, the rabies tracing shows only 'sparse' LC labeling (C38), and it's noted that rabies virus may have labeling biases (C107). The conclusion is well-supported but the sparse connectivity suggests the LC-UBC dopaminergic connection may be modulatory rather than a major input.

results.result: Electrical stimulation of cerebellar inputs (50 stimuli at 50 Hz) elicits monoamine release onto UBCs, as detected by GRABDA2h sensor fluorescence increases that are blocked by Drd2 antagonist L-741,626 (4.88-fold reduction).
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C41-C42 demonstrate monoamine release using the GRABDA2h sensor with appropriate pharmacological validation. The Drd2 antagonist control (C42) is critical as GRABDA2h is a Drd2-based sensor. However, electrical stimulation lacks specificity and activates all inputs to lobule X, so this doesn't definitively identify the source as LC. The result supports monoamine release but requires optogenetic experiments for source identification.

results.result: Optogenetic activation of LC axons (200 pulses at 39 Hz) elicits time-locked increases in GRABDA2h fluorescence in a subset of UBCs (5/20 cells, 25%), with an average success rate of approximately 40% across responding cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C43-C45 provide direct evidence for LC-mediated monoamine release using cell-type-specific optogenetics. The low response rate (25% of cells, 40% trial success in responding cells) is notable and honestly reported. The bimodal response pattern (C44, Figure 5G-H) suggests heterogeneity in LC-UBC connectivity. Controls excluding TH+ Purkinje cell labeling strengthen specificity. However, GRABDA2h can respond to both dopamine and norepinephrine (C110), so this doesn't definitively prove dopamine release.

results.result: Optogenetic stimulation of LC fibers increases UBC firing rate by 1.2 Hz (26% above baseline) in cell-attached recordings with extensive pharmacological isolation, and this effect is abolished by Drd1 antagonist, supporting dopaminergic signaling.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C48 provide the strongest evidence for dopaminergic (rather than noradrenergic) signaling from LC to UBCs through extensive pharmacological controls blocking adrenergic, glutamatergic, and other receptors. The Drd1 antagonist control (C48) is critical. However, the effect size is modest (1.2 Hz, 26%) compared to bath-applied SKF81297 (2.48 Hz, 110%), and NMDA receptors were blocked in these experiments (C114), which may reduce the effect. The result is well-controlled but suggests dopamine is one of multiple neuromodulatory mechanisms.

results.result: Purkinje cells directly inhibit Drd1+ UBCs, with 46% of UBCs (11/24) receiving short-latency GABAergic IPSCs (average latency 9.4 ms, amplitude 91 pA) in response to optogenetic Purkinje cell activation, with a trial success rate of 0.64.
results.evaluation: Claims C9, C56-C60 demonstrate direct Pkj-to-UBC inhibition with appropriate controls (gabazine abolishes IPSCs, C60) and pharmacological isolation of Golgi cells (mGluR2 agonist). The short latency (9.4 ms) supports monosynaptic connectivity. The connectivity rate (46%) and trial success (0.64) are reasonable for cerebellar circuits. This finding, combined with parallel work (C123), establishes a recurrent Pkj-UBC circuit.

results.result: Drd1+ UBCs and Purkinje cells form a recurrent circuit where optogenetic UBC activation causes Purkinje cells to pause (28% of cells) or burst (7%), with pausing correlated with lower EPSC/IPSC ratios (R²=0.63), suggesting the circuit can bidirectionally modulate vestibulo-cerebellar output.
results.evaluation: Claims C10, C51-C55, C119, and C138 demonstrate bidirectional UBC-Pkj connectivity with functional consequences. The correlation between EPSC/IPSC ratio and pausing (C55, R²=0.63) provides mechanistic insight into on-beam/off-beam parallel fiber effects. However, the majority of Pkj cells showed no response (64%, C51), and the experiments were done in acute slices which may underestimate in vivo connectivity. The authors appropriately acknowledge slice limitations in the Discussion.

results.result: Rabies virus tracing reveals that Drd1+ UBCs receive diverse presynaptic inputs including Purkinje cells, Golgi cells, cerebellar nuclei neurons (majority), vestibular nuclei neurons, and sparse LC neurons, with no labeling from midbrain dopaminergic nuclei.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C38 and C40 provide comprehensive input mapping using modified rabies virus tracing with appropriate helper viruses. The finding that cerebellar nuclei provide the majority of inputs (C40) is consistent with prior literature (C108). The sparse LC labeling (C38) is consistent with the low GRABDA2h response rate (C44). However, the authors acknowledge potential biases in rabies virus labeling (C107), and semicircular canal inputs were not assessed (C106).

results.result: Optogenetic activation of Drd1+ UBCs causes bursts of 2-5 action potentials per pulse, with decreased spike number across the stimulus train, indicating adaptation or depression.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C50 characterize UBC responses to optogenetic stimulation, showing burst firing and adaptation. This is consistent with known UBC physiology and provides important context for interpreting downstream Purkinje cell responses. The data are straightforward and well-presented.

results.result: LRN neurons, which form mossy fiber inputs to the cerebellum, express minimal dopaminergic machinery (19/135 express Th, 2/135 express Slc18a2) and are therefore unlikely to be a source of cerebellar dopamine.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C28, C98-C99 exclude LRN as a dopamine source through FISH analysis and anatomical characterization. The quantification is clear and the conclusion is well-supported. This is an important negative control given that Dat-Cre;tdT+ axons in cerebellum originate from LRN (C26).

results.result: The Drd1-Cre;tdTomato mouse line used in this study does not show tdT expression in cerebellar nuclei, in contrast to a different Drd1-Cre line reported in prior literature.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C87 document an important difference between Cre lines that affects interpretation. This is appropriately noted and helps explain discrepancies with prior literature (C86). The observation is straightforward and well-documented.

results.result: The overlap between tdT+ and mGluR1+ UBCs is incomplete (65% of mGluR1+ UBCs express tdT), and only 12.5% of calretinin+ UBCs express tdT, indicating that Drd1 expression defines a specific UBC subpopulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C83 provide important quantitative characterization of the Drd1+ UBC population relative to established UBC markers. The incomplete overlap with mGluR1 (C82) and minimal overlap with calretinin (C83) help define the Drd1+ population. The data are clear and well-quantified.
